site.name: Positive
site.intro: Five small retellings from India’s living story traditions. Read one, then return to your day a little lighter.

stories.title: The Cave That Spoke First
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: One evening a jackal came home to his cave and saw enormous footprints crossing the threshold. Fearing a lion waited inside, he did not rush in but stood at the mouth and called out brightly, as though the rocky walls always greeted him when he arrived.

Deep in the darkness, the lion heard the cheerful voice and assumed the cave had stayed silent only because it was afraid of his strength. Wanting to be kind, he let out a great roaring welcome to reassure the little traveler at his door.

The jackal heard the lion's roar, smiled at his small trick, and slipped away unharmed into the soft evening. Caution, quick thinking, and a kind voice had saved him, and he padded home to a safer den as the stars came out.

stories.title: Hope Finds Its Way Home
stories.source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: King Nala lost Nishadha in a ruinous dice game and was driven far from Queen Damayanti. Yet hardship could not smother their hope of reunion. Damayanti announced a second svayamvara, while Nala, disguised as the charioteer Bahuka, traveled toward the place where her summons might lead him.

When they met again, Nala and Damayanti recognized one another through familiar signs of character and shared memory. Their loyalty endured through separation and disguise. Nala had also learned secret dice knowledge from King Rituparna, and with this new skill he challenged his brother Pushkara once more.

This time Nala won fairly and recovered his kingdom of Nishadha. Instead of seeking revenge against Pushkara, he forgave him. Nala, Damayanti, and their children returned to a peaceful royal life, their family restored and the bitterness of the past released at last.

stories.title: Three Friends by the Lake
stories.source: Panchatantra — Arthur W. Ryder translation (1925), Internet Archive
body: Beside a quiet lake lived three close friends: Shell-Neck the turtle, Slim the mouse, and Grim the crow. When hunters came crashing through the reeds, Grim took to the sky and Slim darted into the grass, but Shell-Neck was caught fast in a hunter's net.

Without hesitation, Slim crept back and gnawed the tough cords until Shell-Neck crawled free. Not long after, Slim himself was trapped in another net, and this time the three worked together. Grim lifted Shell-Neck in his beak and set him on the path ahead, where the turtle lay still as if helpless.

The hunter reached for the seeming prize, and in that moment Slim slipped from the loosened cords. All three friends made their way home to the lake, grateful and joyful that each one's different gift had saved the others.

stories.title: Savitri's Courage Wins Back Satyavan
stories.source: Mahabharata — Vana Parva, Kisari Mohan Ganguli translation
body: Princess Savitri chose the exiled prince Satyavan as her husband, even though a prophecy foretold he would die within a year. When the fateful day arrived, she kept her fast and walked beside him into the forest, where he fell while cutting wood. From his body rose Yama, the lord of death, come to carry away his soul.

Savitri followed Yama through the forest, and as they journeyed she spoke with such clear intelligence and steady devotion that he offered her boon after boon. She asked first for her father-in-law Dyumatsena, restoring his lost sight and his kingdom. Next she won heirs for her own father, King Ashvapati, ensuring his royal line.

Finally Savitri asked for children with Satyavan, and because Yama had promised, he could not refuse. The lord of death returned Satyavan's life, and the young prince awoke beside his faithful wife. Together they walked home, where both families rejoiced, their fortunes restored by her steadfast love.

stories.title: Ahalya Rises at Rama's Touch
stories.source: Valmiki Ramayana — Bala Kanda (Gita Press translation)
body: Walking the forest path with Sage Vishvamitra, Rama and Lakshmana come upon the still and overgrown hermitage of Gautama. The sage tells them that Ahalya, unseen for years beneath a curse, has been waiting there for Rama's coming, when at last her long stillness might end.

Stepping through the doorway at the sage's word, Rama finds Ahalya and speaks gently, and her form emerges into the light again, soft and whole. When Gautama returns and sees her restored, he welcomes her back, and the gods in the sky honor the compassion that has lifted the hermitage out of its long silence.

The lonely clearing fills once more with quiet life, and the separated couple stands together beneath the trees. What had been a forgotten place becomes a home again, and the travelers continue on, carrying with them the warmth of a reunion that grace made possible.
